summary: The Concentration calculator works out molarity. It uses the mass of solute (Mass volume percent (w/v%)), the concentration (Mass volume percent (w/v%)), the mass of solute (Mass percent (w/w%)) and the mass of solution. It suits a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Concentration calculator work?
sections.html:
The Concentration calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports molarity in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the mass of solute (Mass volume percent (w/v%)), the concentration (Mass volume percent (w/v%)), the mass of solute (Mass percent (w/w%)) and the mass of solution.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Concentration calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Molarity=(1 ÷ 100) × density of the solution × percentage concentration by mass ÷ molar mass of solute
Mass per 100 g of water (H₂O)=-percentage concentration by mass ÷ (10 × percentage concentration by mass − 1000)
Moles of solute=volume of solution × concentration (molarity)
Mass of solute=molar mass of solute × moles of solute
Desired concentration=initial concentration × initial volume ÷ required volume
Volume of solution=100 × mass of solute ÷ concentration

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Mass, opening in grams

  • Mass, opening in grams
  • %, opening in percent

  • Molar mass, opening in grams per mole
  • Volume, opening in liters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Concentration calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the mass of solute (Mass volume percent (w/v%)), the concentration (Mass volume percent (w/v%)) and the mass of solute (Mass percent (w/w%)) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Concentration calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns molarity, derived from the mass of solute (Mass volume percent (w/v%)), the concentration (Mass volume percent (w/v%)) and the mass of solute (Mass percent (w/w%)). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Concentration calculator?
faq.a: The form has 14 fields, each listed with its unit in the article above. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mass of solute (Mass volume percent (w/v%)) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mass of solute (Mass volume percent (w/v%)) opens in grams and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Concentration calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
